newsitem.title: UK: Frenchwoman dies of human "mad cow" disease.
newsitem.headline: Frenchwoman dies of human "mad cow" disease.

text.p: French doctors reported a second possible case of a human strain of mad cow disease on Friday, describing a French woman who died of Creutzfeldt-Jakob Disease.
They said they were not sure, but it appeared she had died from a newly identified strain of CJD that scientists say was most likely caused by eating infected beef.

Twelve people -- one French and the rest British -- have died of the new strain, which was publicly identified in March. New biochemical evidence published last month linked the new strain of CJD with Bovine Spongiform Encephalopathy (BSE or mad cow disease).

"A 52-year-old woman from Savoie was referred to a neurology department in March, 1995, with progressively evolving impairment of walking," Nicolas Kopp of the Hopital Neurologique in Lyon wrote in a letter to the Lancet medical journal.
Her symptoms got worse until she could barely speak or stand, and she died five months later.
Kopp said his team reviewed her case from records and brain samples, which indicated she had died of the new variant of CJD.

The new strain is usually characterised by fast progression, unique brain lesions, and a targeting of victims under the age of 40. But some of the victims of the deadly brain illness, which usually strikes one in a million, are older.
In a second letter to the Lancet, German doctors said a man who used to eat animal feed had died of CJD.
Scientists believe the BSE epidemic in British cattle herds started when cows were fed the ground-up remains of sheep infected with scrapie -- their own version of the disease.
Rendered animal remains are routinely fed to farm animals, except in Britain, where the practice is now banned.
The 66-year-old German victim had probably died of one of the naturally occurring strains of CJD, J Weis and colleagues at the Rheinisch-Westfalische Technische Hochschule wrote.

They said the eating habits of the man, who traded in animal feed, might be of interest, however. "According to his family members, he had occasionally tasted samples of the feed to check the quality of the ingredients," they wrote.
"In addition, family members reported that the patient used to prepare for personal consumption a gelatinous material from bovine bones and bone marrow almost daily for several years."
Surveys across Europe have shown that farmers and others who handle animal feed have no higher incidence of CJD than the rest of the population.
